Saturday, 13 December 2036, 3:20 p.m., at the Alliance française. Haruka has given her monologue about machine translation. Now comes the debate with the two examiners, Mrs Lefort and Mr Abadie.
Thank you, mademoiselle. You claim we should keep learning languages. But with machine translators, what’s the point?
That’s an interesting question. I grant you that these tools are very useful for reading a menu or asking the way.
But a machine translates words. It doesn’t translate what isn’t said: irony, politeness, silences.
Machines are progressing very fast. In ten years they may understand irony.
If I’ve understood correctly, you mean that learning will become pointless? I don’t think so.
Even if a machine translated perfectly, it couldn’t learn in my place. And it’s by learning that we change.
Can you give an example?
Yes. Three months ago I couldn’t understand the radio. Today I understand my neighbours’ jokes. No app would have given me those neighbours.
Yet many people don’t have time to learn. Don’t you find your position a little… privileged?
(she thinks) You’re right on one point: not everyone has the same opportunity. That’s why learning should be free and accessible.
But if I may, that isn’t an argument against languages. It’s an argument for teaching them better.
(she smiles) Very good. One last question: why French, for you?
Because one day someone played me three notes on the other side of a door. And I wanted to be able to answer them with words.

1. The DELF B2 speaking paper
The paper is marked out of 25. You get a short document (an article, a news item) that raises an issue:
Duration
you read the document, find the issue, make a plan
5–7 minutes
you present the issue and defend your point of view
10–13 minutes
you answer the examiner’s questions and objections
Don’t summarise the document! It’s only a starting point. The examiner wants to hear YOUR opinion, with arguments.
2. Structure of the monologue
The document I chose deals with… (introducing the topic)
It raises the following question: … (the central question)
I will first show that…, then… (announcing the plan)
Firstly… Secondly… Finally… (the arguments)
To conclude, I would say that… (the conclusion)
In the 30 minutes of preparation, don’t write a whole text: write only the plan and keywords. If you read, the examiner will stop you.
3. Playing for time and rephrasing
Silence isn’t a catastrophe, but it’s better to fill it with natural phrases:
Phrases
to play for time
C’est une question intéressante… Laissez-moi réfléchir… Comment dire…
when you don’t understand
Pardon, pourriez-vous reformuler ? Si j’ai bien compris, vous voulez dire que… ?
when you can’t find the word
Je ne trouve pas le mot… c’est une sorte de… ce qu’on utilise pour…
to correct yourself
Pardon, je voulais dire… Enfin, plus exactement…
Don’t be afraid to correct yourself. Examiners appreciate a candidate who notices a mistake and fixes it.
4. Answering objections
The examiner will play devil’s advocate. They aren’t being aggressive: they want to see whether you can argue:
I grant you that, but… (conceding partly)
You’re right on one point: … On the other hand… (nuancing)
I understand your point of view, but I maintain that… (holding your position)
If I may, that isn’t quite accurate. (disagreeing politely)
Typical mistake: changing your mind completely at the first objection. You can nuance, but don’t abandon everything. A reasoned opinion is worth more than a candidate who agrees with everything.
5. Stage fright and silences
Breathe before you start. (three slow breaths)
Look at the examiners. (not just at your sheet)
Speak slowly. (stage fright makes you speed up)
A pause is not a failure. (breathe, then carry on)

De l’autre côté de la vitre

At Gérard’s café at noon there were more people than usual for a snowy Saturday. Isabelle had told everyone during the writing paper. Julien and Ioana had come with the children. Inès and Sami were there, as were Amina, Bertrand and Awa, bundled up in a red snowsuit that made her look like a little tomato. The six members of the op-ed club hadn’t gone home. Gérard had pushed three tables together. He had made vegetable soup for everyone.

Gérard’s soup had a history. It was Odile’s recipe, which she had given him one winter years before, when he fell ill and she brought him a saucepan of it every day for a week. Leeks, potatoes, carrots, and a secret he had never wanted to reveal to anyone. He said this soup gave you courage. Isabelle tasted it. She said it was exactly her mother’s soup, and she hadn’t eaten it for ten years.

Haruka couldn’t eat. She told them the writing topic, and everyone laughed, like Isabelle. Rose-Hélène said it must have been Grandma Odile who chose the topic, from up there. Haruka also told them about Farid, the Afghan boy, and the rice cake shared at the break. Ioana said that might be the most important thing of the whole morning. Haruka didn’t understand why. Ioana said she would understand later.

Henri-Ion, who had been listening to the whole conversation while eating his bread, gave his own advice for the oral. He said that if Haruka didn’t know what to say, she should just talk about dinosaurs, because everyone loved dinosaurs, even examiners. Haruka promised to think about it. Bernard Delorme arrived at that moment, late, covered in snow. In thirty seconds, very fast, he described his disastrous bus journey. Haruka understood everything. She said it was a good sign.

The speaking paper began at half past two. First, half an hour’s preparation, alone, in a small room. Then twenty minutes in front of two examiners: a five-to-seven-minute monologue, then a debate. Haruka had watched dozens of videos of candidates. She knew the procedure by heart. What she didn’t know was whether her voice would obey her. In the oral mock exam three weeks earlier she had got fifteen out of twenty-five. She had spoken too fast, and she had read her notes.

Ioana had prepared her for the oral in the last week, on top of Inès’s training. Every evening, on the landing, she played the examiner. She asked hard questions, contradicted Haruka, pretended to disagree. On the first evening Haruka changed her mind at every objection. Ioana told her an examiner wasn’t trying to make her change her mind. They wanted to see whether she could defend it. Concede a little, yes. Give up everything, never.

On the third evening Ioana raised the most classic objection: “English is enough. Why learn other languages?” Haruka stammered at first. Then she found it: in Lyon, Bernard Delorme didn’t speak a word of English, nor did the baker, and Gérard even less. If she had spoken only English, she would never have got to know any of them. Ioana applauded. She said that was exactly the kind of concrete example examiners loved: personal, true and impossible to contradict.

Julien had taught her something else: breathing. He had given concerts for twenty years and had stage fright before every one. He showed her how to breathe before speaking: three slow breaths from the belly, as before playing the first note of a concerto. He told her to look at the examiners, not her sheet. And to speak slowly, much more slowly than she thought necessary. Stage fright always made you speed up. You had to brake on purpose.

Inès had given her one last piece of advice for the monologue. She said never to start with an abstract sentence like “Nowadays technology plays an important role”. Examiners heard that thirty times a day. You had to start with a story. An image. Something true that woke people up. She said that in eloquence contests you won or lost in the first thirty seconds. Haruka asked which story to tell. Inès said: “Yours.”

At twenty past two Haruka got up from the table. Everyone got up with her. Gérard gave her a last tea in Odile’s cup. Rose-Hélène came over. She took Henri’s harmonica out of her pocket, the one she never lent to anyone. She wanted to give it to her. Haruka refused. She said she couldn’t take it into the exam room, it wasn’t allowed. Rose-Hélène thought about it. Then she said: “Then I’ll keep it. But I won’t be far.”

Crossing the corridor of the Alliance française, Haruka passed Farid, who was waiting his turn on a chair, his little round stone in his hand. His oral was right after hers. They looked at each other. They didn’t say anything, because the invigilator was there. Farid just raised the stone very slightly, the way you raise a glass. Haruka raised Odile’s pencil. It was a tiny gesture. But for the first time Haruka felt she wasn’t the only foreigner in that corridor.

At half past two an invigilator showed Haruka into a small room on the second floor of the Alliance française. There was a table, a chair, a clock, and a window overlooking the inner courtyard, white with snow. The invigilator presented two sealed envelopes. She had to draw one, then choose between the two documents inside. Haruka drew the left-hand envelope. She opened it. There were two short texts, half a page each.

The little room was cold. The radiator under the window rattled like a saucepan but gave out almost no heat. The clock above the door ticked very loudly, like the one in the writing room. Haruka kept her coat round her shoulders. She put Odile’s pencil and Jeanne Valmont’s bookmark on the table next to the envelope. She took three breaths, as Julien had taught her. Then she opened the documents.

The first text was about the four-day week in companies. The second was titled: “Machine translation: the end of foreign languages?” Haruka skimmed both, as Hortense had taught her. Then she chose the second without hesitating. She thought of her phone on the first day, at the bakery, when the translation app had been no use at all in front of the baker. She thought that on this subject she had something to say. Something true.

She had hesitated for a second all the same. The four-day week was an easier, more neutral topic, with obvious arguments on both sides. Inès had told her always to choose the topic she had personal examples for, even if it seemed harder. You could always find arguments. Real examples, no. Haruka had never worked a four-day week. But for three months she had lived exactly what the second document described. She had examples for an hour.

She read the text carefully. An American university was closing its languages department because phones translated everything. Some found that logical. Others thought a language wasn’t just a code. The final question was clear: should we still learn foreign languages in the age of artificial intelligence? Haruka took Odile’s pencil. She made a plan on the rough paper. Not sentences: words. As Inès had taught her.

Introduction: the bakery, the first day. Central question: learn or translate? First argument: a language carries what isn’t said — irony, politeness, silences. Example: Bernard Delorme, his “hein” and “ben”, impossible to translate. Second argument: learning means being transformed. Example: herself, three months ago and now. Conclusion: a machine translates sentences, it doesn’t create ties. Opening: the fox in The Little Prince, and the word “tame”.

Then she noted three possible objections, as Ioana had advised. “Machines will improve.” “Not everyone has time to learn.” “English is enough.” For each she noted an answer in three words. Then she looked at the clock. Eight minutes left. She went over her plan under her breath, without really reading it, looking out of the window. In the courtyard the snow was still falling. There was nobody there. Just a bench covered in white and an old lime tree with bare branches.

While she waited, she thought of her grandmother in Kyoto, where it was eleven at night. She pictured her sitting in her kitchen in front of her cup of tea, thinking of her, as she had promised in her letter. She thought that on the other side of the world someone was waiting for her too. Then she thought of Odile, whom she had never known, and whose pencil she had been carrying for three weeks. She said under her breath, in French: “I’m going to answer.” The invigilator came in.

At three o’clock the invigilator led her to the exam room at the end of the corridor. It was a bigger room, with a wooden table, three chairs and a large window that also looked out on the snowy courtyard. Two examiners were waiting. A woman of about sixty, with short grey hair and round glasses, who smiled as she held out her hand. And a younger man, about thirty, in a navy jumper, who didn’t smile at all. He was taking notes.

The light from the snow came through the big window and made the room very white, almost unreal. Mrs Lefort wore a red scarf, which she had kept on despite the heating. She looked like a retired primary teacher, and Haruka later learnt that she was: she had taught French to foreign children for thirty-five years at a school in Vénissieux. Mr Abadie was a teacher at the Alliance française. He had the reputation of being the toughest examiner in Lyon.

The woman introduced herself: Mrs Lefort. The man: Mr Abadie. Mrs Lefort explained the procedure in a gentle voice. First Haruka would present the document and her point of view for five to seven minutes without being interrupted. Then they would discuss it together. She added that Haruka could look at her notes, but not read them. Haruka nodded. She put her sheet on the table. She took three slow breaths from the belly, as Julien had taught her. Then she looked up at the examiners.

She began with the bakery. The first day in Lyon, phone in hand, translation app open, and the baker asking her a question too fast. She told them about breakfast for six. Mrs Lefort smiled. Even Mr Abadie raised an eyebrow. Then Haruka presented the document: the American university, the closure of the department, the controversy. She stated the central question. She announced her plan. Her voice was calm. She spoke slowly. Everything was going well.

Her first argument went smoothly. She explained that a language carried more than words. Irony, politeness, innuendo. She talked about Bernard Delorme and his “hein”, without naming him, just “a neighbour who plays the trumpet”. She said no machine could ever translate a Lyonnais “hein”, because it meant ten different things depending on the tone. Mrs Lefort laughed out loud. Mr Abadie wrote something down. Haruka felt time was passing very fast.

Meanwhile, in the courtyard, they had been waiting for a quarter of an hour. It was Isabelle’s idea. That morning she had seen that the oral room looked onto the inner courtyard. She had asked the Alliance française caretaker whether they could wait there in silence. The caretaker refused at first. Then he recognised Gérard: he had had his coffee at his café every morning for twenty years. He opened the gate. He only asked them not to make a sound. They promised.

Then she came to the second argument. She opened her mouth to say that learning a language meant being transformed. She wanted to use a precise word, the word for the act of learning, the process. A word she had read a hundred times. And suddenly the word wasn’t there any more. Her head emptied all at once, like a room when the light goes out. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She looked at her sheet. The word wasn’t there. She hadn’t written it down.

In the courtyard, Rose-Hélène had taken command. She had signalled to everyone to be quiet, a finger to her lips, with the same authority as when she held Amina’s timer. Nobody dared move. Even Awa, in her red snowsuit, watched the window without a sound, as if she understood. Snow fell on their shoulders, their hair, Isabelle’s umbrella. Bernard Delorme, for the first time in his life, had been voluntarily silent for ten minutes. Gérard said later that was the real miracle of the day.

The silence began. One second. Two seconds. Three. Haruka could feel her heart pounding in her ears. She thought of Sorina in Cluj, whose hands had stopped in the middle of a Chopin ballade and who had walked out of the room. She thought of Ioana in 2027, who had nearly been eliminated. Four seconds. Mr Abadie looked up from his notes. Mrs Lefort waited patiently, saying nothing. Five seconds. And that was when Haruka looked out of the window.

In the courtyard, under the snow, there were people. They were there. All of them. Standing in the snow, in silence, next to the old lime tree. Isabelle with her umbrella. Julien and Ioana. Inès and Sami. Amina with Awa in the red snowsuit, Bertrand holding a flask. Gérard, in his apron, who had closed his café. The members of the op-ed club. And in front of them all, tiny in her coat, Rose-Hélène, holding Henri’s harmonica without playing it. They made no sound. They were waiting.

From the courtyard they had seen Haruka stop. They had seen her open her mouth with no sound coming out, then look at her sheet, then stay motionless. Ioana had taken Julien’s hand. Inès had murmured: “Breathe.” Isabelle had said very quietly that nobody must move. And Rose-Hélène, eyes fixed on the window, had started counting on her fingers without a word. One, two, three. As for the third verse. As if she knew exactly how long that silence would last.

That was what Isabelle had meant. In the oral she wouldn’t be alone. They couldn’t come in, couldn’t speak, couldn’t help her. They could only be there, on the other side of the glass, the way Odile had been there, on the other side of a door, for a young Romanian woman who couldn’t find her words. Six seconds. Haruka understood that this silence wasn’t an end. It was the third verse. Eight bars. She counted in her head. Seven. Eight.

Then she took a breath and carried on. She said: “Excuse me. I’m looking for the word. It’s what you do when you learn, little by little, over a long time…” Mrs Lefort waited. Haruka searched for another second. Then the word came back by itself, like a note returning after a pause: “Learning. There. Learning a language transforms us.” Mrs Lefort nodded, very slightly. Mr Abadie wrote something down. Haruka never knew what.

In the courtyard, when they saw Haruka start speaking again, nobody applauded, because they had promised not to make any noise. But Rose-Hélène turned to the others with a huge smile and whispered, so softly that only those next to her heard: “She answered.” Isabelle had to wipe her eyes with the corner of her scarf. Gérard blew his nose loudly. The caretaker at the gate glared at him.

After that, everything became easy. She talked about her three months in Lyon. The radio she couldn’t understand, then could. Cartoons with an eight-year-old girl. A five-year-old boy who had whistled outside her door one evening when she was crying. A café where six strangers looked for the thesis of an op-ed every morning. She said no app had given her those people. It was by learning the language that she had met them. And they had changed her.

She concluded with the fox in The Little Prince. She said a machine could translate the word “tame”, but it couldn’t tame anyone in our place. Creating ties took time, and that time was precisely learning. She looked at the clock. Six minutes twenty seconds. She stopped. Mrs Lefort said: “Thank you, mademoiselle.” Her voice sounded a little different. Haruka glanced out of the window. Rose-Hélène was giving a thumbs-up.

The debate lasted twelve minutes. Mrs Lefort began with a simple, almost friendly question: what was the point of learning, with machine translators? Haruka answered as Ioana had taught her. First she conceded a little: “I grant you these tools are very useful for reading a menu.” Then she held her position: “But a machine translates words. It doesn’t translate what isn’t said.” Mrs Lefort looked satisfied. Then Mr Abadie took over. His questions were much harder.

He said machines were progressing very fast, and in ten years they might understand irony. Haruka rephrased, to play for time and to be sure she had understood: “If I’ve understood correctly, you mean that learning will become pointless?” He said yes. She answered with a sentence she had prepared on the landing with Ioana, which came to her at exactly the right moment: “Even if a machine translated perfectly, it couldn’t learn in my place. And it’s by learning that we change.”

Mr Abadie didn’t give up. He said, in a slightly provocative tone, that many people had neither the time nor the money to learn a language, and that Haruka’s position was a little privileged. It was the objection she hadn’t foreseen. She said: “That’s an interesting question. Let me think.” She thought for three seconds. She thought of Farid, who had taught himself French in a hostel from library books. She thought of Leïla. Of Jeanne Valmont. Then she answered.

She said he was right on one point: not everyone had the same opportunity. She herself had been lucky enough to study, to have a grandmother who was a teacher, to be taken in by a family. But she added: “If I may, that isn’t an argument against languages. It’s an argument for teaching them better, free, to everyone.” She talked about the La Duchère media library, where anyone could borrow books without paying. Mr Abadie put down his pen. For the first time, he smiled.

Mr Abadie had one more objection. He said English was enough anyway for travelling anywhere in the world. Haruka smiled inwardly: it was the objection she had prepared with Ioana. She said English was enough for travelling, but not for living. In her building in Lyon nobody spoke English: not the little girl opposite, not the café owner, not the trumpeter. She said: “With English I would have visited Lyon. With French I live in it.” Mr Abadie wrote the sentence down.

Mrs Lefort looked at the clock. She said there was one minute left and she had a last, more personal question. She asked: “Why French, for you?” Haruka looked out of the window. In the courtyard, under the snow, Rose-Hélène was still holding the harmonica. Haruka turned back to the examiners. She said: “Because one day someone played me three notes on the other side of a door. And I wanted to be able to answer them with words.” There was a silence. A real one.

Mrs Lefort took off her glasses. She wiped them with a corner of her scarf. Then she put them back on. She said, in a perfectly professional voice, that the paper was over and the results would be published online in about five weeks. She added that she wasn’t allowed to comment on candidates’ performances. Then, as Haruka was getting up, she said very quietly, so quietly that Mr Abadie may not have heard: “I’ve seen the film. Twice.”

In the corridor, on her way out, she passed Farid again, who was getting up to go in. He was very pale. She stopped in front of him for a second. She wasn’t allowed to talk to him about her paper. So she just said: “Look out of the window, if you need to.” Farid didn’t understand. He went into the room. Haruka ran down the stairs, wondering whether she had been right to say that.

Haruka ran down into the courtyard. They were all there, covered in snow, red-cheeked, their feet frozen. They had been waiting for forty minutes. Nobody asked how it had gone. Rose-Hélène ran to her and jumped into her arms. Then she played the three notes on the harmonica, in the middle of the courtyard, in the snow. Haruka answered by whistling. Off-key, for the first time in her life. She had perfect pitch, but that day she whistled off-key on purpose.

They stayed in the courtyard. Haruka explained quietly that another candidate, an Afghan boy, was now taking his oral in the same room, and that he was alone in France. Nobody needed to say more. They all stayed there, in the snow, in silence, for another twenty minutes, in front of the window. They didn’t know Farid. They didn’t even know what he looked like. But they stayed. Rose-Hélène said that with the waltz, you didn’t choose who you answered.

Then another voice whistled. A man’s voice, a little hesitant, from the door of the Alliance française. The next three notes. Everyone turned round. It was Farid. He was coming out of his oral, his coat too thin for the weather, his little round stone in his hand. He knew the waltz. He had seen the film “Répondre” in his hostel the year before, on an old computer, with twenty other young refugees. He hadn’t known the waltz came from here. He hadn’t known Haruka knew it.

Farid said later that during his oral he had gone blank in the middle of the monologue. He had remembered what Haruka told him. He had looked out of the window. And he had seen, in the courtyard, under the snow, about twenty people he didn’t know, standing in silence, watching him. A little girl had given a thumbs-up. He hadn’t understood who they were. But he had understood they were there for him. He took a breath. He carried on.

Haruka introduced him to everyone. Farid was intimidated by all these people, by Rose-Hélène asking whether he could play the harmonica, by Bernard Delorme, who had arrived in the meantime and talked to him too fast. Ioana went over to him. She asked where he lived. He said he lived in a hostel in Villeurbanne with thirty other young people, and had no family in France. Ioana looked at Haruka. Haruka understood what Ioana had meant at the café at noon.

At dinner that evening Farid told a little of his story. Not all of it. The long, dangerous journey he didn’t want to describe. Arriving in France at seventeen, alone. The hostel in Villeurbanne. The library books he borrowed three at a time. The first book he had read all the way through in French, with a dictionary, in two months: “The Little Prince”. Haruka put down her fork. She asked whether he remembered the fox. Farid recited without hesitating: “One sees clearly only with the heart.”

Ioana invited Farid to dinner that same evening at the rue d’Austerlitz. Then to the orchestra the following Thursday. Then to Christmas. Farid accepted all three invitations, blushing a little more each time. Bertrand lent him a warmer coat. Amina opened a new spreadsheet. Gérard told him the tea at the café would always be on the house. And Rose-Hélène promised to teach him the harmonica, on condition that he taught her an Afghan word every week in return. Farid said that at home they spoke Dari. Rose-Hélène said that suited her fine.

The following Thursday Farid came to the orchestra. He didn’t play any instrument. Théo asked him what he would like to do. Farid said he would just like to listen. Bernard Delorme had a better idea. He entrusted him with the foghorn for the fifth bar of the silence, with very precise and far too fast instructions. Farid didn’t understand everything. When the silence came he pressed the horn a second too early. The whole hall burst out laughing. So did Farid. Bernard said he was hired.

The five weeks of waiting were long. Haruka spent Christmas at the rue d’Austerlitz, at Julien and Ioana’s, with Isabelle, Farid, and a video from Kyoto in which her grandmother, in a kimono, whistled the three notes in front of a plastic Christmas tree Aoi had put up for the occasion. On New Year’s Eve she played the waltz on the landing at midnight, with Rose-Hélène on harmonica and Farid whistling. The neighbours upstairs knocked on the ceiling. Then they came down in their pyjamas with a bottle of champagne.

At Christmas Rose-Hélène gave Farid a small red plastic harmonica, exactly like the one she had given Awa when she was born. She had bought it with what was left of her savings. Farid couldn’t play it. She taught him the first three notes that very evening on the landing. In return he taught her his first word of Dari: “tashakor”, which meant thank you. Rose-Hélène wrote it in her notebook, next to Henri-Ion’s Romanian words and Haruka’s Japanese ones.

The results were published on Friday 16 January 2037 at nine in the morning on the Alliance française website. Haruka didn’t want to look at them alone. She went down to Gérard’s café at half past eight. They were all there, once again. The op-ed club, Isabelle, Julien, Ioana, the children before school, Inès, Sami, Farid, Amina, Bertrand and Awa, who was eight months old now and could stand holding on to chairs. Gérard had switched on the café’s old computer.

Over the five weeks Haruka had checked the Alliance française website every day, even knowing the results weren’t there. Amina had finally forbidden it, with a spreadsheet calculating the time wasted looking at an empty page: four hours twelve minutes in a month. Hortense Valmont had sent her a New Year card. On it she had written a single word in Japanese characters, clumsily traced with a brush: “ma”. Haruka had stuck it on her wall, next to Bernard’s record.

At nine on the dot Haruka typed in her candidate number. The page took an eternity to load. Nobody spoke. All you could hear was the hum of the fridge and Awa’s little noises. Then the page appeared. There were four lines and a total. Listening: twenty-one. Reading: twenty-two. Writing: twenty-one. Speaking: nineteen and a half. Total: eighty-three and a half out of a hundred. Underneath, in green: “Passed”.

Haruka didn’t react straight away. She reread the figures once, then twice, like an op-ed whose thesis you’re looking for. Then she looked at the speaking line: nineteen and a half. The lowest of the four. She thought of the eight seconds of silence, the word that had flown away, the window. She thought that nineteen and a half was the mark she was proudest of. Because it was the one where she had almost lost everything. And where someone, on the other side of the glass, had helped her answer.

The café exploded. Gérard slapped the counter. The old Latin teacher shouted something in Latin. Rose-Hélène played the three notes very loudly. Inès hugged Haruka, saying she had always known. Amina filled in a cell of her spreadsheet, in green too. And Farid, looking at his own phone, gave a cry. He had got sixty-four. He had passed too. He could start nursing school in September. He sat down on a chair and cried, his little stone clutched in his hand.

Farid called the nursing school from the café, his voice shaking. The secretary confirmed that with his certificate, his enrolment was accepted for September. He hung up. He looked at everyone, these people he hadn’t known five weeks earlier. He said, in his hesitant French, that he had left his country three years ago, and this was the first time he had a family to tell good news to. Ioana hugged him. Nobody said anything else.

It was at that moment, amid the noise, that it happened. Awa, standing against her father’s chair, let go of the chair. She took one step, just one, towards Bertrand. Then she looked up at him with her big serious eyes and said, very clearly, in the middle of the café: “Papa.” Everyone fell silent at once. Bertrand knelt down. He couldn’t speak. Amina took out her phone with a trembling hand and opened the “Nous” file at the “First word” column.

She wrote: “Papa. 16 January 2037, 9:04 a.m., Gérard’s café. First step too.” Then she added a line to the other spreadsheet, the one that had compared Awa and Haruka for three months: “Final result: a draw.” Haruka burst out laughing. She said Awa had won, because her first word was harder to say than the DELF. Bertrand, still crying, said it was the most beautiful word in the French language. Hortense Valmont, to whom Haruka sent a message, replied that she agreed.

That day, leaving the café, Haruka called Mrs Lefort. She had found her number through Isabelle, who knew someone who knew the school in Vénissieux. She only wanted to thank her. Mrs Lefort said she hadn’t done anything, she had only waited. Then she added that in thirty-five years of teaching she had learnt one thing: her pupils’ most beautiful silences were always the ones that came before an answer. Haruka said she knew someone who would have agreed. A neighbour, long ago.

On Monday 19 January Haruka presented herself at the conservatoire with her certificate. The secretary, the same one who had spoken too fast in September, looked at the paper, then at Haruka, then at the paper again. She spoke to her at the same speed as in September. Haruka understood everything. She answered at the same speed. The secretary looked surprised. Then she smiled and said: “Welcome, Miss Mori.” Haruka said it was the first time anyone in Lyon had pronounced her name correctly first time.

In the afternoon she had her first violin lesson, with an old white-haired teacher, Mr Delattre, who had trained generations of violinists. He asked her to play something of her choice. Haruka hesitated, then played the waltz. At the third verse she stopped. Eight bars. Mr Delattre said nothing. He waited, eyes closed. Then Haruka started again. At the end the old teacher opened his eyes. He said: “You have understood the essential. The rest I can teach you.”

The following Thursday, at rehearsal, Théo announced to the orchestra that he had two pieces of news. The first: Haruka had passed the DELF B2 and was starting at the conservatoire. The second: Farid had passed too, and would start nursing school in September. The whole hall stood up to applaud. Bernard Delorme sounded the foghorn, which set off the school alarm for the third time that year. The caretaker came running. He saw the faces. He switched off the alarm. He said nothing.

That same evening she wrote her grandmother a letter. A real letter, in French, three pages long, with a plan, connectors, long sentences and short ones, as Sami had taught her. She told her everything: the snow, the exam room, the word that had flown away, the eight seconds of silence, and all those people standing in the courtyard on the other side of the glass. She knew it would take her grandmother a month to read it, with her dictionary and Aoi’s help. She wrote it anyway. At the end she added a single line in Japanese: “I answered.”

Traduction automatique : la fin des langues étrangères ?

An American university has just announced the closure of its foreign languages department. According to its president, students no longer need to learn Spanish or Chinese: their phones now translate in real time into more than a hundred languages.
The decision has sparked heated controversy. For some, it is logical: why spend years learning what a machine does in a second? The time saved could be used for other subjects.

For others, on the contrary, it is a serious mistake. A language is not just a code: it carries a culture, a way of thinking, a sense of humour. Machines translate sentences, but not always what lies between the lines.
Education specialists also point out that learning a language develops memory, patience and openness to others. Qualities no app can offer.
Should we still learn foreign languages in the age of artificial intelligence? Present your point of view with reasoned arguments.
